questions.q: What is the quickest way to create a circuit with 3 qubits and 2 classical bits?
questions.explain: QuantumCircuit's constructor takes qubit count first, then classical bit count: QuantumCircuit(3, 2) gives 3 qubits and 2 classical bits.

questions.q: Why would you build a circuit from explicit QuantumRegister/ClassicalRegister objects instead of just QuantumCircuit(n)?
options: It's required for any circuit with more than 1 qubit
It lets you name and group qubits/bits, which helps readability once a circuit combines multiple logical groups
It changes the mathematical result of the circuit
questions.explain: Named registers don't change what a circuit computes — they make diagrams and multi-register circuits easier to read by labeling which qubits belong to which logical group.

questions.q: What does qc.draw('mpl') do differently from qc.draw()?
options: It simulates the circuit and returns measurement counts
It renders a graphical Matplotlib diagram instead of the default text diagram
It converts the circuit to OpenQASM
It only works on circuits with measurements
questions.explain: Both produce a diagram of the circuit's structure; the default draw() renders plain text, while draw('mpl') renders a graphical version using Matplotlib.

questions.q: A brand-new QuantumCircuit(3) has had no gates added yet. What is qc.depth()?
options: Undefined until a gate is added
questions.explain: depth() counts the longest chain of sequentially-dependent operations. With no gates at all, there's nothing sequential to count, so depth is exactly 0.

questions.q: What does num_qubits tell you about a QuantumCircuit?
options: How many gates have been applied so far
The total number of qubits the circuit was constructed with
The number of possible measurement outcomes
questions.explain: num_qubits is a fixed structural property set when the circuit is created — it reflects how many qubits exist, not how many gates have been applied or what depth the circuit has reached.
